title: ‘We said no, no, no, but they kept insisting’: the Paraguayan people battling a eucalyptus empire
summary:
It is Paraguay’s largest private investment but local people accuse a forestry giant of ignoring their contamination concerns over its vast plantation

When Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

Photograph: Matteo Fabi Southern frontlines: Latin America and the Caribbean Global development ‘We said no, no, no, but they kept insisting’: the Paraguayan people battling a eucalyptus empire It is Paraguay’s largest private investment but local people accuse a forestry giant of ignoring their contamination concerns over its vast plantation Supported by About this content Laurence Blair in Concepción, Maximiliano Manzoni in Asunción, and Marcello Rossi in Parma. Photographs and video by Matteo Fabi Tue 10 Nov 2026 06.00 EST Last modified on Tue 10 Nov 2026 06.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs. “They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people. But today, the minimum-wage work often dwindles and the well stops working during power cuts. More worrying are its eucalyptus plantations, which begin less than 200 metres from the community’s crops and homes. The community of Tacuarita is now surrounded by eucalyptus plantations. Video: Matteo Fabi Paracel is made up of the Paraguayan Zapag group, the Austrian pulp producer Heinzel and Swedish forestry company Girindus Investments. The project is expected to be the largest private investment in Paraguay’s history. The company will reportedly invest about $5bn (£3.7bn) and create 7,000 jobs , mainly in the northern region of Concepción. Financed by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and Paraguay’s government , the company says it is protecting existing ecosystems while “reforesting” former ranchland with 162m eucalyptus trees to fight global heating. View image in fullscreen Santiago Peña, Paraguay’s former president, second left, with Per Olofsson, Paracel chair, centre, and former vice-president and now president, Pedro Alliana, in Paso Horqueta. Photograph: VP's office It is also building an industrial plant to process these non-native trees – which already cover an area larger than New York City – into pulp for the global paper and packaging industry. Paracel was championed by the then-president Santiago Peña, who headlined the construction launch of the company’s pulp mill in May. Peña was removed from office and arrested this month over the collapse of Ueno Bank. He denies any wrongdoing. Though unrelated to Paracel, the case has cast uncertainty over the signature projects of his administration. But an investigation by the Guardian with the local media outlets Consenso and the Paraguay Post , has documented accusations of water contamination, harmful pesticide use, worsening drought, land disputes and forced evictions in 12 communities. Paracel is a “hidden monster that has quietly taken root”, says Benjamín Valiente, a human rights defender who works for the local Catholic diocese. “They’re murdering nature for profit.” View image in fullscreen Benjamín Valiente, a human rights defender who says the Catholic church is one of the few institutions to oppose Paracel. Photograph: Matteo Fabi Official documents indicate that the plantations are being treated with sulfluramid , an insecticide that degrades into a “forever chemical” linked to cancer in humans. Sulfluramid is banned in the EU , one of Paracel’s two main export markets , along with China . Paracel says it had “no record” of staff saying water near Tacuarita would be contaminated by its chemicals, as one of the company’s representatives had allegedly told the community. In a 39-page response to a request for comment, the company highlighted its “significant contributions to economic, social and environmental development in the area”. Meanwhile, farmers in the town of Puentesiño, near Paracel’s plantations, accuse the company of occupying land earmarked for people living in poverty 50 years ago by presidential decree
